chapter: Piano craft and the New York school
title: Jelly Roll's orchestral piano style
summary: Debate whether Morton played stride; Ramirez says he played orchestral, like a band; the contrast between Wild Bill Davis and Jimmy Smith.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: But I think this is one of the troubles all along with Jazz, that you have these vagues or fashions whereby something is automatically considered old-fashioned. Now, my theory was that Jelly Roll Morton sort of came more out of the... He had more relationship to Earl Hines than he did to that stride style. Well, Jelly Roll Morton didn't really play stride.
Jelly Roll played stride, but he played orchestral.
You know, he played orchestral, but he played like a band. And I think his... I've never read books, but the opinion goes that you don't necessarily have to sound like a band to play Jazz.

And that is true. Say, for instance, you play your left hand, you have rhythmic patterns, and the tenor range and the alto range is one, and then the upper voices carry the melody, and then the accompaniment. And that is the basis of Jazz... Modern music, you know. Any kind of music.
Well, you can play like a band on a keyboard instrument. That's the difference, say, between Wild Bill Davis and Jimmy Smith.
You see? Wild Bill plays a band, Jimmy Smith plays like a horn. Well, now, Earl can do either. He can play like a horn in the treble, or he could play very good stride, too.
